sent: Meet Aoife and Conor. They've rented in Dublin for four years.
Rent is €1,800 a month, and a baby is on the way.
Tonight they're scrolling listings, and the same questions keep going round their heads.
How much can we actually borrow?
Is our deposit big enough?
Are there schemes to help us?
What are the hidden costs?
And what happens if rates go up?
Step one: know your number.
Central Bank rules: first-time buyers can usually borrow up to 4× gross income.
Together they earn €110,000, so about €440,000.
Lenders also expect a 10% deposit.
Step two: the deposit.
They have €22,000 saved and add €800 a month.
Our deposit calculator shows the date: about 1 year 11 months. Save a little more and it gets closer.
Step three: use the help that exists.
Help to Buy: refund of income tax and DIRT paid, up to €30,000, on a new build.
First Home Scheme: shared equity, up to 30% of a new home or 20% second-hand, within price limits.
Local Authority Home Loan: a backstop if a bank says no. Each has conditions, so check early.
Step four: the costs nobody puts in the advert.
Stamp duty is 1% up to €1m. Then legal fees, valuation and a survey.
Lenders also require mortgage protection and home insurance.
Budget roughly €9,000–€12,000 on top of the deposit.
Step five: get approval in principle before you view.
It sets your budget, shows sellers you're serious, and usually lasts 6 months.
€360,000 over 30 years at 4% is about €1,719 a month.
If rates rise 1%: €1,933, which is €214 more. Better to know now.
Step six: protect the plan.
Mortgage protection clears the loan if the worst happens.
An emergency fund of 3–6 months of essentials stops one bad month becoming a crisis.
